name: Wilson's temperature syndrome

card.summary: A proposed condition of low body temperature and fatigue-type symptoms, treated by some practitioners with cyclical sustained-release T3 in the hope of restoring energy, leaner body composition, and better hair and skin.
card.note: Not recognised as a diagnosis by the American Thyroid Association; the protocol involves prescription thyroid hormone and a physician was disciplined over it in 1992.

quick.overview:
Wilson's temperature syndrome (WTS) is a condition proposed in 1990 by Florida physician E. Denis Wilson. It describes low oral body temperature together with symptoms such as tiredness, dry hair and skin, hair thinning, fluid retention and difficulty losing weight, despite normal standard thyroid blood tests. People interested in it are usually looking to recover energy for training, leaner body composition, and healthier hair and skin.

Wilson's proposed explanation is that stress leaves thyroid hormone conversion stuck in a low-output mode, and that a temporary course of sustained-release T3 'resets' it. The American Thyroid Association rejected the concept in 2005, and a single small published report on the protocol exists. The idea circulates in forums on TRT and thyroid optimisation.
quick.how: Proponents describe tracking oral temperature several times a day with a thermometer, comparing the average to 98.6 F, and, under a physician, using a cyclical sustained-release T3 schedule that is adjusted to temperature and later tapered. Details are set by prescribers and are not covered here.
quick.risks: T3 is a prescription thyroid hormone. The American Thyroid Association says the syndrome's criteria are imprecise and non-specific, and excess thyroid hormone can cause heart rhythm problems and bone loss. In 1988 a patient of Wilson's died of an arrhythmia and heart attack after taking large amounts of oral thyroid hormone, and in 1992 the Florida Board of Medicine disciplined him.

lead: Wilson's temperature syndrome (WTS), also called Wilson's syndrome, is a condition proposed by E. Denis Wilson, a physician in Longwood, Florida, who coined the term in 1990 [1]. It links a low average oral body temperature and a broad set of complaints, including fatigue, headaches, mood changes, hair loss, dry skin and hair, and weight gain, to a reversible slowdown in how thyroid hormone is used by the body, even when standard thyroid blood tests are normal [1][2].

In appearance-focused communities the topic comes up among people trying to recover energy for training, lose stubborn weight, and address thinning, dry hair and skin. On forums such as T Nation, members dealing with low testosterone, cold extremities, dry brittle hair and fatigue mention WTS as a possible explanation and discuss temperature-guided T3 protocols [3][4].

The protocol Wilson pioneered (often called WT3) uses cyclical dosing of sustained-release liothyronine (T3), adjusted to the patient's temperature response and then withdrawn once temperature has stayed at about 98.6 F [5]. A 2006 article described the protocol and its use in the complementary medicine community [5]. The American Thyroid Association issued a statement in 2005 saying the syndrome conflicts with established thyroid physiology and that its criteria are imprecise [6].

chain: Low body temperature and low energy attributed to impaired T3 activity

angle.text: People who describe the syndrome link its symptoms, such as dry brittle hair, weight that will not shift and fatigue, to appearance and training goals. The claimed route to looking better is restoring a normal temperature and metabolism through a prescriber-supervised T3 course.

paras: Proponents describe WTS as a functional condition in which a stressful event, illness or dieting period leaves the body producing more reverse T3 (rT3), an inactive form, relative to active T3, lowering cellular thyroid activity and body temperature [7]. Because the blood tests used in conventional thyroid diagnosis stay normal, supporters say temperature charting and symptom review are the way to identify it [7].

Reported symptoms include fatigue, headaches, depression, fluid retention, difficulty losing weight, dry skin, dry hair, irritability, low libido and insomnia [7]. Several of these (hair, skin, weight) are why the topic reaches appearance-focused readers.
Wilson coined the name in 1990 and published a book on it in 1992 [1]. He held that the diagnosis could be confirmed by improvement on sustained-release T3 [1].

In 1988 one of his patients, aged 50, died of an arrhythmia and heart attack after taking excessive oral thyroid hormone. In February 1992 the Florida Board of Medicine took disciplinary action; Wilson accepted a six-month licence suspension, continuing education, a fine, and an agreement not to prescribe thyroid medication unless the Board found the medical community had accepted his concept [1].

On internet forums, WTS appears in threads on thyroid and testosterone. Users recommend it to one another, mention rT3, and compare it with other dosing approaches such as the 'circadian T3 method' [3][8][9].

Supporters hold that average temperature below 98.6 F, measured with a glass thermometer several times a day, is the key objective marker [7]. Forum members describe tracking morning temperatures and attempting multi-week versions of the protocol [10]. Dosing is determined case by case by prescribers and is not described here.

A 2006 paper in the Puerto Rico Health Sciences Journal described the WT3 protocol: sustained-release T3 taken every 12 hours on a cyclic schedule set by patient response, with weaning after a temperature of 98.6 F is maintained [5]. It is a description of clinical practice in complementary medicine. No randomised controlled trial of the protocol has been identified, and the syndrome has no accepted diagnostic criteria in endocrinology [1][6].

The American Thyroid Association statement of 24 May 2005 said the syndrome conflicts with established knowledge of thyroid function and called its diagnostic criteria imprecise and non-specific [1][6]. Endocrinologists note that normal body temperature varies between people and through the day, and that fatigue, low mood and similar symptoms have many causes [7].

Over-replacement with thyroid hormone is associated with palpitations, arrhythmia and bone loss, and the 1988 death and 1992 disciplinary case are part of the record [1][7]. T3 is prescription-only in most countries.

lore.intro: Wilson's temperature syndrome is raised on T Nation threads about low testosterone, fatigue and thyroid labs, usually as a suggestion from one member to another [3][4][8].

claims.claim: Low body temperature plus high reverse T3 shows a thyroid problem that normal tests miss
claims.believers: Forum members point to temperatures such as 97.4 F or below and symptoms like dry brittle hair and cold extremities as signs [2][10].
claims.experts: The American Thyroid Association calls the criteria imprecise and non-specific, and notes natural variation in body temperature [6][7].

claims.claim: A temporary T3 course can reset metabolism so the person no longer needs medication
claims.believers: Wilson's followers say temperature normalises and is then held after weaning [5]. Forum users describe attempting the protocol [10].
claims.experts: A 2006 paper describes the protocol but no controlled trial has been published [5]. Over-replacement is associated with heart and bone harms [1][7].

claims.claim: Temperature can guide thyroid hormone dosing
claims.believers: Forum members suggest using body temperature as the guide to adjusting T3 [4].
claims.experts: Endocrine guidance relies on blood tests and clinical assessment rather than temperature charts [6].
